opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that we have to stop assuming the model is going to be the thing that keeps us safe. For a long time in security we've had this principle that you don't trust any single component, and I think we need to apply that to language models too. Right now there's a tendency to say, "Well, the model has been trained to refuse bad instructions, so it'll probably be fine." But we've spent the better part of a decade showing that essentially every machine learning model is vulnerable to adversarial inputs, and I don't see any reason to believe that's suddenly going to change just because the models got bigger.

So if you accept that the model can be tricked, and I think you should, then the question becomes: how do you design a system where it doesn't matter that much when it gets tricked? That's a very different engineering question. It means thinking about privilege separation. If an agent is reading untrusted emails or web pages, maybe that same agent shouldn't also have the ability to send money or delete your files. You can have one component that sees the untrusted data but has very limited capabilities, and another component that has the capabilities but never sees the raw untrusted text. There's been some nice work along these lines, and it looks a lot more like traditional systems security than like machine learning.

It also means being realistic about where agents should be deployed. If the worst-case outcome of a successful attack is that the agent writes a slightly wrong summary, that's probably fine. If the worst case is that someone exfiltrates your entire inbox or drains your bank account, you need a much higher bar, and today I don't think the models alone meet that bar. Having a human confirm the high-stakes actions, limiting what tools are available, logging everything so you can audit after the fact. None of this is glamorous, but it works.

The thing I worry about is that the capabilities are improving faster than the defenses, and there's a lot of economic pressure to give these agents more and more autonomy. People will say the attack success rate went from 50% to 5%, and that sounds great. But in security, 5% is not a fix. If an attacker can try a hundred times, 5% means they win. We need to measure robustness against adaptive attackers who are actually trying to break the system, not against a fixed benchmark of attacks someone wrote last year.

So my view is cautiously pragmatic. I'm not saying don't build agents. I use these models every day and they're enormously useful. But build them the way you'd build any system that has to handle hostile input: assume the component will fail, and make sure the failure is contained.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that you don't get to assume the model is secure, and you have to design the system as if it isn't. That's actually not a new situation in security. We've never had secure components. We've never had a C compiler that was bug-free, or a web browser that couldn't be exploited. What we do have is forty years of experience building systems where we assume individual pieces will fail and we try to limit the blast radius when they do.

So the way I'd frame it is: the model is the untrusted component. Anything that comes out of the model, you should treat the way you'd treat input from a user on the internet. If the model says "run this command," that's not an instruction from a trusted insider, that's a request from something that might have been manipulated by whatever text it read thirty seconds ago. And once you adopt that stance, a lot of the classical tools start to apply. Least privilege: don't give the agent credentials it doesn't need for the task. Sandboxing: run it somewhere where the worst thing it can do is bounded. Separating the plane that reads untrusted data from the plane that takes consequential actions, so that the thing reading your emails isn't the same thing with the ability to send money.

The place where this gets genuinely harder than classical security is that the attack surface is natural language. With SQL injection we eventually got parameterized queries, where you could cleanly separate code from data. We don't have that for language models. There's no way to tell the model "this part is instructions and this part is just data, don't follow anything in it," because the whole point of the model is that it reads everything and reasons about all of it. Every mitigation I've seen for prompt injection makes attacks harder, which is good, but none of them makes attacks impossible. And in security, "harder" is not the same as "solved." An attacker who's motivated will spend the time.

So I'm fairly pessimistic about the idea that we'll make the models themselves robust in the near term. I've spent a lot of my career breaking defenses that people were confident in, and adversarial robustness in machine learning has been an open problem for over a decade with, frankly, not a lot of progress on the core question. What I'm more optimistic about is the systems-level work. If you can arrange things so that a successful attack on the model gets you something small and recoverable rather than something catastrophic, you've won most of the battle. That's much less glamorous than a clever defense that makes the model immune, but it's the thing that actually works.

The thing I'd push back on is the instinct to deploy agents with broad capabilities first and worry about this later. Right now we're in a window where the attacks are mostly demonstrations by researchers. That won't last. The moment there's real money attached to manipulating an agent, people will do it, and they'll be a lot more creative than the academic papers. I'd rather we build the guardrails now, while the cost of getting it wrong is embarrassment rather than something worse.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to separate two questions: can we make the model harder to attack, and can we build a system that remains secure when the model gets attacked? We should work on both, but I wouldn’t want the security of the entire system to depend on getting the first one perfectly right.

Suppose I have an agent that reads my email and helps manage my calendar. Reading an email shouldn’t give that email’s author the ability to tell the agent to send them all my other emails. The difficulty is that the model sees both the legitimate task and the attacker’s instructions as text. So I want something outside the model enforcing what information it can access and what actions it can take.

We already do versions of this in computer security. We sandbox programs. We give them limited permissions. We assume that a component might be compromised and try to limit the damage. We should apply that same thinking to agents: give them only the capabilities they need, and put checks around consequential actions that an attacker can’t simply talk the model into bypassing.

That doesn’t solve everything. If the agent’s job is to summarize a document and the document tricks it into producing a misleading summary, a permission boundary won’t necessarily help. But it can keep a bad summary from turning into a stolen account or leaked database. That’s a useful distinction. Dependability has to come from the whole system, rather than from an assumption that the model will always follow the right instructions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to stop assuming that the model has to be secure in order for the system to be secure. In computer security, we build systems out of components that can fail, and then we put boundaries around what those failures can do.

If you have an agent reading arbitrary web pages, you should assume that, at some point, a page is going to convince it to do something you didn’t intend. Then ask: What can it actually do? Can it read your private files? Can it send those files somewhere? Can it spend money? Those permissions need to be enforced by something outside the model. Asking the model to please follow the security policy isn’t an access-control mechanism.

The hard part is that we want agents to be useful, and usefulness often requires access. So I don’t think there’s a single fix here. You give the agent narrowly scoped permissions, isolate sensitive operations, and require approval where a mistake would be consequential. And you test the whole system against an attacker who’s actively trying to break it.

We should absolutely keep trying to make models more robust. But I’d be much more comfortable with a system whose safety argument is, ‘Even if the model gets tricked, the damage is limited,’ than one whose safety argument is, ‘We think the model won’t get tricked.’
